bartlett-filter.detail: Before saying yes, ask whether it moves you closer to the person you want to become.
bartlett-filter.episode: Why we're getting more depressed, anxious and lonely
bartlett-filter.title: The yes test

bartlett-nature.detail: Build a longer walk somewhere green into every week.
bartlett-nature.episode: Why we're getting more depressed, anxious and lonely
bartlett-nature.title: Regular time in nature

candow-creatine.caveat: Tell your GP you take it, as it can raise creatinine on blood tests. Check first if you have a kidney condition.
candow-creatine.detail: One scoop a day, any time, with anything. Pick a third-party tested product. It's one of the most researched supplements, for muscle and possibly the brain.
candow-creatine.episode: Creatine is the fat loss secret
candow-creatine.title: 5 g creatine monohydrate daily

candow-strength.detail: Two whole-body sessions a week is the baseline. Lighter weights taken close to failure also work.
candow-strength.episode: Creatine is the fat loss secret
candow-strength.title: Strength train at least twice a week

clear-prep.detail: Lay out gym kit, leave the book on the chair, write the first line of tomorrow's task.
clear-prep.episode: Your goals are quietly restricting your happiness
clear-prep.research: A behavioural design principle from Atomic Habits.
clear-prep.title: Set up tomorrow tonight
clear-prep.why: Clear's point is that motivation is lowest at the moment you need to start, so you make starting easier in advance. Laying out your clothes, filling the water glass or opening tomorrow's first task the night before removes a decision from the morning.

clear-review.detail: Once a month, check whether your routines are still moving you towards what you want, and adjust.
clear-review.episode: Your goals are quietly restricting your happiness
clear-review.title: Monthly systems review

clear-stack.detail: Attach the new habit to an existing one: after I make my coffee, I'll sit in silence for 60 seconds.
clear-stack.episode: Your goals are quietly restricting your happiness
clear-stack.title: Stack it onto something you already do

clear-two-minutes.detail: Cut any habit down to a version that takes two minutes, like just rolling out the mat. Starting is the hard part.
clear-two-minutes.episode: Your goals are quietly restricting your happiness
clear-two-minutes.title: Shrink it to two minutes

comer-community.detail: Eat with people from church or friends you follow Jesus with each week.
comer-community.title: Share a meal with your community

comer-digital-sabbath.detail: Switch the phone off for a set block each week, such as Sabbath evening, to make room for unhurried attention.
comer-digital-sabbath.title: Phone-free block

comer-examen.detail: Look back over the day: where you noticed God, what you're grateful for, and what to bring to him.
comer-examen.research: An Ignatian practice from the 1500s, taught in Practicing the Way.
comer-examen.title: Evening examen
comer-examen.why: The examen is a short look back over the day with God: what you're grateful for, where you noticed him, and what you want to bring to him. It builds awareness and gratitude, and ends the day in prayer rather than on a screen.

comer-fasting.caveat: Check with your GP before fasting if you have a health condition.
comer-fasting.detail: Skip a meal or fast until dinner one day a week, using the hunger as a prompt to pray.
comer-fasting.title: Weekly fast

comer-fixed-hour.detail: Brief prayer at morning, midday and evening, so prayer runs through the day and not just the start.
comer-fixed-hour.research: Christian tradition (the Daily Office), taught in Practicing the Way.
comer-fixed-hour.title: Pray at fixed points in the day
comer-fixed-hour.why: Fixed-hour prayer is the ancient practice of stopping at set points in the day to pray, so prayer runs through the whole day rather than just the morning. A short midday pause, perhaps a psalm, the Lord's Prayer or a few quiet words, breaks the momentum of work and re-centres you.

comer-generosity.detail: Each month, deliberately give money, time or possessions beyond what feels comfortable.
comer-generosity.title: Give something away

comer-sabbath.detail: 24 hours to stop work, rest, delight and worship. Plan it ahead so it actually happens.
comer-sabbath.title: Keep a weekly Sabbath

comer-scripture.detail: Read a short passage slowly, perhaps twice, and notice which line stays with you.
comer-scripture.research: Christian tradition (lectio divina), taught in Practicing the Way.
comer-scripture.title: Slow Scripture reading
comer-scripture.why: Rather than reading a lot quickly, Comer encourages reading a short passage slowly so it shapes you rather than just informs you. Read it twice and notice which line stays with you: a simple form of the old practice of lectio divina. Breakfast, with the phone still away, is a natural moment for it.

comer-silence.detail: Ten quiet minutes with God before looking at a screen. Sit, breathe, and simply be present.
comer-silence.research: A practice from Christian tradition, taught in Practicing the Way.
comer-silence.title: Morning silence before the phone
comer-silence.why: Comer argues that hurry is the great enemy of the spiritual life, and that silence and solitude are where you notice God and your own inner life again. Starting the day quietly, before any input, sets a different pace for everything after it. Sit somewhere comfortable, breathe slowly and simply be with God; when your mind wanders, gently come back.

comer-slowing.detail: Small deliberate choices to slow down: drive in the slow lane, choose the longest queue, walk without rushing.
comer-slowing.title: Practise slowing down

huberman-back-to-sleep.detail: With eyes closed, move your eyes slowly side to side, then take two or three long exhales.
huberman-back-to-sleep.episode: My exact routine to optimise brain & body
huberman-back-to-sleep.title: Can't get back to sleep?

huberman-breathing.detail: Slow breathing with exhales longer than inhales. A couple of long sighs works as a quick reset when stressed.
huberman-breathing.episode: My exact routine to optimise brain & body
huberman-breathing.research: A 2023 Stanford study found five minutes of daily cyclic sighing improved mood more than mindfulness meditation.
huberman-breathing.title: 5 minutes of long-exhale breathing
huberman-breathing.why: Long, slow exhales switch on the body's calming system and lower your heart rate within a minute or two. Huberman suggests a few minutes of breathing where the out-breath is longer than the in-breath, or a couple of 'physiological sighs' (two breaths in through the nose, one long breath out) as a quick reset in the middle of a busy day.

huberman-evening-dim.detail: Catch some late-afternoon daylight, then keep lights low and screens down after dark to protect sleep.
huberman-evening-dim.episode: My exact routine to optimise brain & body
huberman-evening-dim.research: Strong evidence that bright evening light delays melatonin and sleep.
huberman-evening-dim.title: Dim the lights in the evening
huberman-evening-dim.why: Bright overhead light in the evening tells your brain it's still daytime and delays the signals that make you sleepy. Huberman suggests switching to low lamps after dark and turning screens down, to protect your sleep.

huberman-morning-light.detail: Get outside within an hour of waking for 5–20 minutes, with no sunglasses, before you look at your phone. On grey days stay out a bit longer.
huberman-morning-light.episode: My exact routine to optimise brain & body
huberman-morning-light.research: Circadian research on morning light is strong; the exact minutes are rules of thumb.
huberman-morning-light.title: Morning daylight walk
huberman-morning-light.why: Daylight reaching your eyes early sets your body clock: it brings on alertness now and helps you feel sleepy at the right time tonight. Outdoor light is many times brighter than indoor light, even on a cloudy day, so a short walk outside does far more than sitting by a window. Aim for 5–10 minutes on bright days and longer when it's grey.

huberman-water.detail: Start with about 500 ml of water, then aim for roughly 2–2.5 litres through the day.
huberman-water.episode: My exact routine to optimise brain & body
huberman-water.research: General hydration research is solid; the exact amounts are his own routine.
huberman-water.title: Big glass of water on waking
huberman-water.why: You lose water overnight through breathing and sweat, so most people wake up slightly dehydrated. Huberman's point is that even mild dehydration dulls focus and mood, and a big glass first thing is the easiest fix there is. Keep a full glass by the sink so it happens on autopilot.

jessie-savoury-breakfast.detail: Make breakfast protein-led, like eggs or yoghurt, and save sweet things for after a meal.
jessie-savoury-breakfast.episode: The scary new research on sugar
jessie-savoury-breakfast.research: Based on glucose-monitor studies; how much it helps varies between people.
jessie-savoury-breakfast.title: Savoury breakfast
jessie-savoury-breakfast.why: A sweet breakfast, even 'healthy' cereal or juice, sends blood glucose up fast and then down, which often drives the mid-morning slump and cravings. Inchauspé suggests building breakfast around protein, fat and fibre, such as eggs, Greek yoghurt or avocado, with bread as a small side and whole fruit as the only sweet thing.

jessie-veg-first.detail: Start meals with a portion of vegetables before any starch or sugar to flatten the glucose spike.
jessie-veg-first.episode: The scary new research on sugar
jessie-veg-first.research: Small but consistent clinical studies, mostly in people with type 2 diabetes.
jessie-veg-first.title: Eat your veg first
jessie-veg-first.why: The order you eat in changes how fast sugar reaches your bloodstream. Starting with vegetables, then protein and fat, then starch, means the fibre slows down how quickly the glucose is absorbed, so the same meal causes a smaller spike.

jessie-vinegar.caveat: Check with your GP if you're on any glucose-lowering medication.
jessie-vinegar.detail: A tablespoon of vinegar in a tall glass of water before eating.
jessie-vinegar.episode: The scary new research on sugar
jessie-vinegar.research: Small studies show modest reductions in glucose spikes; results vary.
jessie-vinegar.title: Vinegar before a carb-heavy meal
jessie-vinegar.why: A tablespoon of vinegar in a glass of water before a starchy meal slows how quickly the starch turns into glucose in your blood. Inchauspé presents it as an optional extra rather than a must, and it's best taken diluted and through a straw to protect your teeth.

murray-calendar.detail: Book naps, walks, workouts and quiet time like meetings so they don't get squeezed out.
murray-calendar.episode: Overcoming depression, burnout, anxiety and insomnia
murray-calendar.title: Put rest and exercise in the calendar

murray-gratitude.detail: Keep an object somewhere you'll see it each morning and use it as a cue to name one specific thing you're grateful for.
murray-gratitude.episode: Overcoming depression, burnout, anxiety and insomnia
murray-gratitude.title: Morning gratitude prompt

murray-one-habit.detail: Add a single new habit and let it settle before stacking another.
murray-one-habit.episode: Overcoming depression, burnout, anxiety and insomnia
murray-one-habit.title: One new habit at a time

murray-walk.detail: Most days, even in the rain. He calls it his single best habit for mental health.
murray-walk.episode: Overcoming depression, burnout, anxiety and insomnia
murray-walk.title: An hour's walk with no headphones

nicola-4x4.detail: Four hard 4-minute efforts near your max heart rate, with 4 easy minutes between each. Once a week is enough.
nicola-4x4.title: One 4×4 interval session

nicola-air-squats.detail: Ten bodyweight squats when you're back at the desk. It's in the lunch routine so it actually happens; add a set every hour through the afternoon if you can.
nicola-air-squats.research: Good evidence for breaking up sitting; ten squats is a practical number rather than a researched one.
nicola-air-squats.title: 10 air squats for every hour you sit
nicola-air-squats.why: Long stretches of sitting are linked to poorer brain and metabolic health, even in people who exercise. Nicola suggests breaking them up with a quick set of squats, which wakes up the biggest muscles in your body and gets blood moving. Doing it straight after the lunch walk means it actually happens.

nicola-bp.caveat: Take readings to your GP rather than acting on them alone.
nicola-bp.detail: Use an automatic cuff and keep an eye on the trend, aiming near 120/80. She treats blood pressure as a brain-health number, not just a heart one.
nicola-bp.title: Check your blood pressure at home

nicola-heavy-legs.caveat: Build up the load gradually, ideally with a coach checking your form.
nicola-heavy-legs.detail: Squats or deadlifts at a heavy load (around 80% of your one-rep max), two or three times a week. Leg strength is one of the things she links most closely to brain health.
nicola-heavy-legs.title: Heavy leg session

protein-target.caveat: The experts give different numbers, so treat this as a range.
protein-target.detail: Aim for roughly 1.2–2 g of protein per kg of body weight, spread across meals, to hold on to muscle with age.
protein-target.title: Hit a daily protein target

spector-30-plants.detail: Count every distinct vegetable, fruit, grain, nut, seed, herb and spice. Variety matters more than quantity.
spector-30-plants.episode: The new truth about weight loss, calories & diets
spector-30-plants.title: 30 different plants a week

spector-fermented.detail: Kefir, live yoghurt, kimchi, sauerkraut, miso or kombucha. A small amount daily for your gut.
spector-fermented.episode: The new truth about weight loss, calories & diets
spector-fermented.research: A 2021 Stanford trial found a fermented-food diet increased gut microbiome diversity and lowered inflammation markers.
spector-fermented.title: A fermented food every day
spector-fermented.why: Fermented foods contain live microbes that support a more varied gut microbiome, which Spector links to lower inflammation and better overall health. A small daily serving, like a spoon of kefir, live yoghurt, kimchi or sauerkraut, matters more than a big portion now and then.

spector-window.caveat: Results vary a lot between people.
spector-window.detail: For example, eat between 9am and 7pm and nothing outside it. Works for some people better than others.
spector-window.episode: The new truth about weight loss, calories & diets
spector-window.title: Around a 10-hour eating window

williamson-caffeine.caveat: The science behind this is disputed; try it and see if it helps you.
williamson-caffeine.detail: Push your first coffee back to mid-morning to avoid the afternoon slump.
williamson-caffeine.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-caffeine.research: Popular advice, but the evidence is thin and debated. Treat it as an experiment.
williamson-caffeine.title: Wait about 90 minutes before caffeine
williamson-caffeine.why: When you wake, your body is already releasing cortisol to get you going, so the idea is to let that do its job and save caffeine for later in the morning. Williamson says pushing coffee back helps avoid the early-afternoon crash. Try it for a week and see whether you notice a difference.

williamson-dry-90.detail: Run a 90-day experiment without alcohol and notice the effect on sleep, mood and energy.
williamson-dry-90.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-dry-90.title: 90 days alcohol-free

williamson-meal-walk.detail: A short walk after eating, especially after the biggest meal of the day. Chores or calf raises count if you can't get out.
williamson-meal-walk.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-meal-walk.research: Well supported: several studies show short walks after meals lower glucose spikes.
williamson-meal-walk.title: 10-minute walk after meals
williamson-meal-walk.why: Working muscles soak up glucose, so even a gentle 10-minute walk after eating flattens the blood sugar spike and helps digestion. Williamson calls it one of the highest-return habits there is: free, short, and you feel better straight after.

williamson-never-twice.detail: Missing one day is fine. Missing two in a row is how a habit dies, so make the day after a miss non-negotiable.
williamson-never-twice.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-never-twice.title: Never miss twice

williamson-no-phone.detail: Keep the phone out of reach until you're up, washed and dressed, so the day starts on your terms.
williamson-no-phone.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-no-phone.research: A behavioural principle rather than a specific study.
williamson-no-phone.title: No phone until you're ready
williamson-no-phone.why: If the first thing you see is your inbox or the news, someone else sets your mood and agenda before you've decided anything. Williamson's suggestion is to keep the phone away until you're up, washed and dressed, so the start of the day is yours. It pairs naturally with ten minutes of silence.

williamson-phone-out.detail: Use a cheap alarm clock instead, so the phone isn't the last and first thing you see.
williamson-phone-out.episode: Fix this one habit and 2026 will be your best year
williamson-phone-out.research: Studies link phone use in bed to later and poorer sleep.
williamson-phone-out.short: Phone on charge outside the bedroom
williamson-phone-out.title: Charge your phone outside the bedroom
williamson-phone-out.why: If your phone sleeps next to you, it's the last thing you see at night and the first in the morning. Charging it in another room and using a cheap alarm clock protects your sleep and makes a phone-free morning almost automatic.

wright-balance.detail: Switch legs halfway through. A free daily balance drill attached to something you already do.
wright-balance.research: How long you can balance on one leg is a well-studied marker of healthy ageing.
wright-balance.short: Stand on one leg while brushing
wright-balance.title: Stand on one leg while brushing your teeth
wright-balance.why: Balance quietly declines from your 40s if you don't train it, and most serious falls in later life happen from standing. Standing on one leg while you brush your teeth costs no extra time and trains the small stabilising muscles and reflexes you'll rely on later. Swap legs halfway; close your eyes to make it harder.

wright-impact.caveat: Build up slowly if your joints aren't used to it.
wright-impact.detail: Finish your walk with ten jumps, skips or hops. Short bursts of impact load your bones, and it's easy to tag onto a walk you're already doing.
wright-impact.research: Impact exercise for bone density is well supported. Start gently if your joints aren't used to it.
wright-impact.title: 10 jumps to finish your walk
wright-impact.why: Bones respond to impact: they get stronger when they're loaded with sudden force and weaker when they aren't. Wright's point is that muscle work and a good diet aren't enough on their own; you also need to jump, hop or skip. Ten jumps after your walk is a small, regular dose.

wright-vitamin-d.caveat: Ask your GP for the test and the right dose.
wright-vitamin-d.detail: Test first, then supplement to a maintenance dose and retest, rather than guessing.
wright-vitamin-d.title: Get your vitamin D tested

wright-warmup.detail: A few minutes of dynamic movement such as jumping jacks or inchworms to move every major joint before training.
wright-warmup.title: Joint-by-joint warm-up

d-pause.cue: Close the laptop and step away
d-pause.name: Pause work

m-ready.cue: Shower, brush your teeth, get dressed
m-ready.name: Getting ready
